description: The commands that measure a drawing, set up the drafting environment it is built in, gather objects into selection sets, and model and document in three dimensions. Most have a command-line or hyphen-prefixed form that works in scripts and macros, and nearly every setting they change is readable and writable as a system variable with getvar and setvar.

tools.name: DIST
tools.description: Measure the distance and angle between two points. It reports the straight-line distance, the angle in the XY plane, the angle from the XY plane, and the delta X, Y and Z components, so it answers both 'how far' and 'in what direction' in one go. The result is left in the read-only DISTANCE system variable, which is how a LISP routine picks the value up.
tools.usage:
DIST  (alias DI)
Specify first point: <point>
Specify second point or [Multiple points]: <point> | M
Distance = ...,  Angle in XY Plane = ...,  Angle from XY Plane = ...
Delta X = ...,  Delta Y = ...,  Delta Z = ...

parameters.name: first point / second point
parameters.description: The two points to measure between, normally picked with object snaps so the result is exact.

parameters.name: Multiple points (M)
parameters.description: Keep picking points and accumulate a running total distance along the chain, with an Arc and Length option for curved legs.

parameters.name: DISTANCE
parameters.description: Read-only system variable holding the last distance computed; (getvar "DISTANCE") returns it.

parameters.name: UCS
parameters.description: Angles are reported relative to the current UCS X axis, so a rotated UCS changes the reported angle but not the distance.

tools.example:
; Exact centre-to-centre distance between two holes
DIST
cen
(pick first circle)
cen
(pick second circle)

; AutoLISP: read the result back
(command "_DIST" '(0 0) '(300 400))
(princ (getvar "DISTANCE"))   ; => 500.0
tools.notes: DIST is the same engine as the Distance option of MEASUREGEOM, which is the command Autodesk now documents as the general inquiry tool. Use the (distance p1 p2) AutoLISP function instead when you only need the number and not the command-line report.

tools.name: AREA
tools.description: Calculate area and perimeter, either from points you pick around a shape or directly from a closed object. The Add area and Subtract area modes keep a running total, which is how a floor area with courtyards or a plate with cut-outs is measured in one session. Results are stored in the AREA and PERIMETER system variables.
tools.usage:
AREA  (alias AA)
Specify first corner point or [Object/Add area/Subtract area] <Object>: <point> | O | A | S
(Add mode) Specify first corner point or [Object/Subtract area]:
Area = ...,  Perimeter = ...
Total area = ...

parameters.name: Object (O)
parameters.description: Measure a closed object directly: circle, ellipse, closed polyline, polygon, region, spline or 3D solid. Far more accurate than picking corners.

parameters.name: Add area (A)
parameters.description: Switch to add mode; every subsequent area or object is added to a running total that is reported after each pick.

parameters.name: Subtract area (S)
parameters.description: Switch to subtract mode; areas picked or selected are removed from the running total.

parameters.name: AREA / PERIMETER
parameters.description: Read-only system variables holding the last computed area and perimeter.

parameters.name: open polylines
parameters.description: An open polyline is treated as if a straight segment closed it for the area, but its perimeter is reported as the real, open length.

tools.example:
; Net floor area: whole room minus two columns
AREA
A
O
(select the room polyline)
S
O
(select the first column)
O
(select the second column)


; AutoLISP: read the result back
(command "_AREA" "_O" (entlast))
(princ (getvar "AREA"))
tools.notes: Use BOUNDARY first when the shape is made of overlapping lines and arcs: it traces one closed polyline that AREA Object can then measure exactly. MEASUREGEOM ARea offers the same Add and Subtract modes with on-screen feedback, and MASSPROP gives area plus centroid and moments for regions.

tools.name: MASSPROP
tools.description: Report the mass properties of selected regions or 3D solids. For a region it gives area, perimeter, bounding box, centroid, moments and products of inertia, radii of gyration and the principal moments about the centroid; for a solid it gives mass, volume and the same inertia data. It is the quickest route to section properties for a structural calculation, and the report can be written to an .mpr text file.
tools.usage:
MASSPROP
Select objects: <regions or 3D solids>
Select objects: Enter
---------------- SOLIDS ----------------
Mass / Volume / Bounding box / Centroid / Moments of inertia / ...
Write analysis to a file? [Yes/No] <N>: Y | N
Enter file name <drawing.mpr>: <path>

parameters.name: Select objects
parameters.description: Regions and 3D solids only. Mixing the two in one selection is not allowed - the first object picked decides which type is analysed.

parameters.name: Write analysis to a file
parameters.description: Saves the report as a plain-text .mpr file that can be pasted into a calculation sheet.

parameters.name: Mass
parameters.description: Computed with a density of 1, so the number equals the volume; multiply by the real density yourself.

parameters.name: Centroid
parameters.description: Reported in the current UCS, so set the UCS to the section's own axes before reading moments of inertia.

parameters.name: Principal moments
parameters.description: Moments about the principal axes through the centroid, with the X-Y-Z directions of those axes.

tools.example:
; Section properties of a plate with two holes
RECTANG
0,0
200,20
CIRCLE
50,10
4
CIRCLE
150,10
4
REGION
ALL

SUBTRACT
(select the rectangle region)

(select the two circle regions)

MASSPROP
L

Y
C:/calc/plate_section.mpr
tools.notes: Because the centroid and the moments are reported in the current UCS, running MASSPROP under a rotated UCS is the standard way to get Ixx and Iyy about a member's own axes. For a quick volume only, MEASUREGEOM Volume is faster.

tools.name: LIST
tools.description: Display the database information held for the selected objects in the text window: object type, layer, space, handle, colour, linetype and lineweight when not ByLayer, plus the geometry - coordinates, radius, length, area, text string, block name and insertion point. It is the fastest way to find out exactly what an object is when the Properties palette does not show enough, and the handle it reports is what LISP and external tools use to address the object.
tools.usage:
LIST  (alias LI or LS)
Select objects: <selection>
Select objects: Enter
(report appears in the text window - F2 toggles it)

DBLIST   ; lists every object in the drawing

parameters.name: Select objects
parameters.description: Any objects; the report is produced one object at a time in selection order.

parameters.name: Handle
parameters.description: The permanent database handle of the object, used by (handent) in AutoLISP and by external data links.

parameters.name: Space
parameters.description: Reports whether the object lives in model space or paper space.

parameters.name: F2 / text window
parameters.description: The report scrolls in the text window; press F2 to show or hide it, or use TEXTSCR and GRAPHSCR.

tools.example:
LIST
(select a polyline)

; Reports: LWPOLYLINE, layer, handle, area, length and every vertex

; AutoLISP equivalent that returns the data as a list
(entget (car (entsel "\nPick an object: ")))
tools.notes: DBLIST lists every object in the drawing and can take a very long time on a large file - press Escape to stop it. Use the Properties palette (PROPERTIES, Ctrl+1) for editable values; LIST is read-only but shows items, such as the handle, that Properties does not.

tools.name: ID
tools.description: Report the X, Y and Z coordinate of a point in the current UCS and store it as the last point. Because the value lands in LASTPOINT, the @ symbol immediately afterwards refers to it, which makes ID the standard way to establish a temporary origin before typing relative coordinates.
tools.usage:
ID
Specify point: <point>
X = ...   Y = ...   Z = ...

; The point is stored in LASTPOINT and is what @ refers to

parameters.name: point
parameters.description: Any picked or typed point; use an object snap to report an exact feature coordinate.

parameters.name: LASTPOINT
parameters.description: System variable holding the coordinate; readable and writable with getvar and setvar.

parameters.name: current UCS
parameters.description: Coordinates are reported in the current UCS, so the same point gives different numbers under a rotated or moved UCS.

tools.example:
; Use a corner as a temporary origin, then work relative to it
ID
int
(pick the corner)
LINE
@0,0
@100,0
@0,50


; AutoLISP
(command "_ID" '(250 175 0))
(princ (getvar "LASTPOINT"))
tools.notes: ID does not create anything - use POINT if a node is wanted. Under a UCS other than World, compare with the coordinate display on the status bar, which also follows the current UCS.

tools.name: MEASUREGEOM
tools.description: The modern combined inquiry command: distance, radius, angle, area and volume from one command, with graphical feedback and a dimension-style read-out on screen. The Quick option (AutoCAD 2020 and later) hovers over geometry and instantly shows the distances, angles and areas it finds without any picking, which is the fastest way to interrogate an unfamiliar drawing. It replaces DIST, AREA and the old inquiry toolbar for most day-to-day work.
tools.usage:
MEASUREGEOM  (alias MEA)
Enter an option [Distance/Radius/Angle/ARea/Volume/Quick/eXit] <Distance>: D | R | A | AR | V | Q | X
(the chosen mode then prompts like the matching standalone command and stays active until eXit)

parameters.name: Distance (D)
parameters.description: Distance, angle and deltas between two points, with a Multiple points option that totals a chain.

parameters.name: Radius (R)
parameters.description: Radius and diameter of a selected arc or circle.

parameters.name: Angle (A)
parameters.description: Angle defined by an arc, a circle, two lines, or a vertex and two points.

parameters.name: ARea (AR)
parameters.description: Area and perimeter, with the same Object, Add area and Subtract area modes as the AREA command.

parameters.name: Volume (V)
parameters.description: Volume of a 3D solid, or of an area extruded through a given height, again with Add and Subtract modes.

parameters.name: Quick (Q)
parameters.description: Live measurement: move the cursor over 2D geometry and the dimensions, angles and enclosed areas appear as you hover. Available from AutoCAD 2020.

tools.example:
; Area of a room, less a service duct
MEASUREGEOM
AR
A
O
(select the room polyline)
S
O
(select the duct polyline)

X

; Volume of a finished solid
MEASUREGEOM
V
O
(select the 3D solid)
X
tools.notes: The results also land in the AREA, PERIMETER and DISTANCE system variables, so scripts can read them the same way as with the older commands. MEASUREGEOM only reports - it creates no objects and no dimensions; use DIM or the dimension commands when the value must appear on the drawing.

tools.name: QUICKCALC
tools.description: Open the QuickCalc palette: a calculator with a number pad, scientific functions, unit conversion, variables and a set of geometric functions that pick coordinates, distances and angles straight from the drawing. Its real value is transparent use - start it while another command is waiting for a number or a point, compute the value, and paste it into the prompt. Values can be stored as named variables and reused.
tools.usage:
QUICKCALC  (alias QC; Ctrl+8; close with QCCLOSE)
'QUICKCALC   ; transparent use inside another command

; Legacy command-line calculator
CAL
>> Expression: (dist(end,end))/2

parameters.name: Number pad / Scientific
parameters.description: Basic arithmetic plus sin, cos, tan, log, exponent and power functions; angles are entered in degrees.

parameters.name: Units conversion
parameters.description: Convert length, area, volume and angular values between unit systems inside the palette.

parameters.name: Variables area
parameters.description: Store constants and expressions (for example a standard wall thickness) under a name and paste them into any prompt.

parameters.name: Geometric functions
parameters.description: Distance between two points, angle of a line, intersection of two lines and the centroid of three points, all picked from the drawing.

parameters.name: Transparent use
parameters.description: Typing 'QUICKCALC at any numeric or point prompt computes a value and returns it to the waiting command.

tools.example:
; Offset by half of a measured distance
OFFSET
'QUICKCALC
(use Distance between two points, divide by 2, then Apply)
(select the object)
(pick the side)

; The legacy calculator does the same at a prompt
CIRCLE
'CAL
(cen+[0,25])
10
tools.notes: CAL is the older command-line geometry calculator and still works; it understands snap functions such as end, mid, cen and int inside expressions. QuickCalc keeps a history list, so a value computed earlier in the session can be pasted again without retyping.

tools.name: UNITS
tools.description: Set how linear and angular values are displayed and entered: the length format and precision, the angle format and precision, the direction of angle zero, whether angles increase clockwise, and the insertion scale unit. It changes display only - the underlying geometry is always stored in full precision, so switching from decimal to architectural never moves anything. The hyphen form -UNITS runs the same settings at the command line and is what scripts use.
tools.usage:
UNITS  (alias UN; command-line version -UNITS)
(dialog) Length: Type [Architectural/Decimal/Engineering/Fractional/Scientific] + Precision
         Angle:  Type [Decimal Degrees/Deg-Min-Sec/Grads/Radians/Surveyor's] + Precision, Clockwise
         Insertion scale: units to scale inserted content
         Direction... : base angle and direction

-UNITS
Enter choice, 1 to 5 <2>:            ; length format -> LUNITS
Enter number of digits to right of decimal point (0 to 8) <4>:   ; LUPREC
Enter choice, 1 to 5 <1>:            ; angle format -> AUNITS
Enter number of fractional places for display of angles (0 to 8) <0>:  ; AUPREC
Enter direction for angle 0 <0>:     ; ANGBASE
Do you want angles measured clockwise? [Yes/No] <N>:   ; ANGDIR

parameters.name: LUNITS
parameters.description: Linear format: 1 Scientific, 2 Decimal, 3 Engineering, 4 Architectural, 5 Fractional - the same numbers as the -UNITS choices.

parameters.name: LUPREC
parameters.description: Number of decimal places, or the denominator of the smallest fraction, used to display linear values.

parameters.name: AUNITS
parameters.description: Angular format: 0 decimal degrees, 1 degrees/minutes/seconds, 2 grads, 3 radians, 4 surveyor's units.

parameters.name: AUPREC
parameters.description: Number of decimal places used to display angles.

parameters.name: INSUNITS
parameters.description: Unit this drawing is drawn in (0 unitless, 1 inches, 2 feet, 4 millimetres, 5 centimetres, 6 metres). Together with the block's own units it drives automatic scaling on insertion.

parameters.name: ANGBASE / ANGDIR
parameters.description: Direction of angle zero (0 = East by default) and whether angles are measured counter-clockwise (0) or clockwise (1).

tools.example:
; Metric drawing set up from a script - no dialog appears
-UNITS
2
3
1
2
0
N

INSUNITS
4

; Read the settings back from AutoLISP
(princ (list (getvar "LUNITS") (getvar "LUPREC") (getvar "INSUNITS")))
tools.notes: UNITS affects display and typed input only; a drawing is unitless internally, which is why INSUNITS matters so much - a mismatch between two drawings is the usual reason a block arrives 25.4 times too large or too small. Dimension text follows the dimension style's own unit settings (DIMLUNIT, DIMDEC), not UNITS, so both have to be set for a consistent sheet.

tools.name: LIMITS
tools.description: Set the rectangular drawing area in model or paper space by its lower-left and upper-right corners, and optionally enforce it so that points outside are rejected. Limits are a legacy of pen plotting but still matter: ZOOM All uses them, the grid traditionally fills them, and a template that sets limits to the sheet size in drawing units keeps everyone working at the right scale.
tools.usage:
LIMITS
Reset Model space limits:
Specify lower left corner or [ON/OFF] <0.0000,0.0000>: <point> | ON | OFF
Specify upper right corner <420.0000,297.0000>: <point>

parameters.name: lower left / upper right
parameters.description: Opposite corners of the drawing area, in the current UCS. Stored in LIMMIN and LIMMAX.

parameters.name: ON
parameters.description: Turn limits checking on: points outside the limits are refused with 'Outside limits'. Stored in LIMCHECK.

parameters.name: OFF
parameters.description: Turn limits checking off (the default) so objects may be drawn anywhere.

parameters.name: LIMMIN / LIMMAX
parameters.description: System variables holding the two corners; settable directly from LISP or a script.

parameters.name: ZOOM All
parameters.description: Zooms to the limits, or to the drawing extents when objects fall outside them.

tools.example:
; A1 sheet at 1:100 in millimetres
LIMITS
0,0
84100,59400
ZOOM
A

; From AutoLISP
(setvar "LIMMIN" '(0.0 0.0))
(setvar "LIMMAX" '(420.0 297.0))
(setvar "LIMCHECK" 0)
tools.notes: Limits checking only rejects points typed or picked inside a command; it does not stop objects arriving by COPY, INSERT or an xref. In current releases the grid extends beyond the limits by default, so the classic 'grid shows the paper size' behaviour needs the GRID Limits option turned on.

tools.name: SNAP
tools.description: Restrict cursor movement to an invisible grid of a given spacing, so points land on exact increments. The Style option switches between the standard rectangular snap and isometric snap, which rotates the crosshairs to the 30/150/90 degree isoplanes for isometric drawing, and the Type option selects rectangular grid snap or polar snap along the polar tracking angles.
tools.usage:
SNAP  (alias SN; F9 or Ctrl+B toggles it)
Specify snap spacing or [ON/OFF/Aspect/Legacy/Style/Type] <10.0000>: <dist> | ON | OFF | A | L | S | T
(Style) Enter snap grid style [Standard/Isometric] <S>: S | I
(Type)  Enter snap type [Polar/Grid] <Grid>: P | G

parameters.name: spacing
parameters.description: Snap increment in drawing units; stored in SNAPUNIT with SNAPMODE holding the on/off state.

parameters.name: Aspect (A)
parameters.description: Different X and Y snap increments, for example 10 horizontally and 5 vertically.

parameters.name: Style (S)
parameters.description: Standard or Isometric. Isometric snap sets SNAPSTYL to 1 and makes the crosshairs follow the current isoplane; F5 or ISOPLANE cycles left, top and right.

parameters.name: Type (T)
parameters.description: Grid snap (rectangular or isometric) or Polar snap, which snaps to increments along the polar tracking angles. Stored in SNAPTYPE.

parameters.name: SNAPANG / SNAPBASE
parameters.description: Rotation angle and origin of the snap and grid, used to align them with a skewed building or a rotated detail.

parameters.name: Legacy (L)
parameters.description: Makes the cursor snap to the grid only while a command is active, restoring the older behaviour.

tools.example:
; 5 mm snap on a 10 mm grid
SNAP
5
GRID
10

; Isometric drafting setup
SNAP
S
I
10
ISOPLANE
R
ELLIPSE
I
0,0
25
tools.notes: Snap spacing and grid spacing are independent; setting the grid to a multiple of the snap is what makes picking predictable. Object snaps (OSNAP) override grid snap when both would apply, which is why exact geometry should be picked with running snaps rather than by trusting the snap increment.

tools.name: GRID
tools.description: Display a reference grid of dots or lines at a given spacing. The modern grid is a line grid with major lines every few minor ones, adapts its density as you zoom out, and can follow the current UCS. It is display only - nothing plots, and the grid does not constrain the cursor, which is what SNAP does.
tools.usage:
GRID  (alias F7 or Ctrl+G toggles it)
Specify grid spacing(X) or [ON/OFF/Snap/Major/aDaptive/Limits/Follow/Aspect] <10.0000>: <dist> | ON | OFF | S | M | D | L | F | A

parameters.name: spacing
parameters.description: Grid interval in drawing units; 0 makes the grid follow the snap spacing. Stored in GRIDUNIT, with GRIDMODE holding the on/off state.

parameters.name: Major (M)
parameters.description: Number of minor grid intervals between major grid lines; stored in GRIDMAJOR.

parameters.name: aDaptive (D)
parameters.description: Limit the grid density when zoomed out, and optionally subdivide it further when zoomed in beyond the grid spacing.

parameters.name: Limits (L)
parameters.description: Confine the grid to the area set by LIMITS instead of filling the whole screen.

parameters.name: Follow (F)
parameters.description: Make the grid follow the XY plane of a dynamic UCS as it changes.

parameters.name: GRIDSTYLE / GRIDDISPLAY
parameters.description: GRIDSTYLE switches between the line grid and the classic dotted grid per space; GRIDDISPLAY is the bitcode behind the adaptive, limits and follow behaviour.

tools.example:
GRID
10
GRID
M
5
GRID
ON

; Classic dotted grid confined to the limits
GRIDSTYLE
1
GRID
L
ON
tools.notes: A grid spacing that is far too small for the current zoom produces the message that the grid is too dense to display; the adaptive option prevents it. Grid and snap are set together on the Snap and Grid tab of DSETTINGS.

tools.name: ORTHO
tools.description: Constrain cursor movement to the horizontal and vertical directions of the current UCS, so lines, moves and copies stay exactly orthogonal. It is the simplest drafting aid there is and it applies to any command that asks for a second point. Polar tracking is the more flexible alternative and the two are mutually exclusive - turning one on turns the other off.
tools.usage:
ORTHO  (F8 toggles it)
Enter mode [ON/OFF] <OFF>: ON | OFF

; Same setting as the system variable
ORTHOMODE  0 | 1

parameters.name: ON / OFF
parameters.description: Enable or disable orthogonal constraint. Stored in ORTHOMODE.

parameters.name: current UCS
parameters.description: Ortho follows the X and Y axes of the current UCS, and of the snap rotation angle SNAPANG, so it can be made to follow a skewed grid.

parameters.name: temporary override
parameters.description: Holding Shift while picking temporarily reverses the current ortho state without changing the setting.

parameters.name: polar tracking
parameters.description: POLARMODE and the polar angle settings in DSETTINGS give alignment at any increment; switching polar tracking on turns ortho off.

tools.example:
; Draw an orthogonal outline by direct distance entry
ORTHO
ON
LINE
0,0
(move the cursor right) 100
(move the cursor up) 50
(move the cursor left) 100
C

; From AutoLISP
(setvar "ORTHOMODE" 1)
tools.notes: With ortho on, direct distance entry - move the cursor in a direction and type a length - is the fastest way to draw rectilinear geometry. In 3D, ortho constrains to the UCS XY plane axes, so set the UCS before relying on it.

tools.name: OSNAP
tools.description: Set the running object snaps: the modes that make the cursor lock onto exact features such as endpoints, midpoints, centres and intersections. The dialog form opens the Object Snap tab of Drafting Settings; the hyphen form -OSNAP takes a comma-separated list at the command line, and the same state is held as a bitcode in OSMODE, which is how scripts and LISP routines save, change and restore the user's settings.
tools.usage:
OSNAP  (alias OS; F3 toggles running snaps; Shift+right-click for the override menu)
(dialog) Object Snap tab of Drafting Settings

-OSNAP
Enter list of object snap modes: END,MID,CEN,NOD,QUA,INT,INS,PER,TAN,NEA,GEO,APP,EXT,PAR
Enter list of object snap modes: NONE      ; clears them all

parameters.name: OSMODE
parameters.description: Bitcode holding the running snaps: 1 Endpoint, 2 Midpoint, 4 Center, 8 Node, 16 Quadrant, 32 Intersection, 64 Insertion, 128 Perpendicular, 256 Tangent, 512 Nearest, 1024 Geometric Center, 2048 Apparent Intersection, 4096 Extension, 8192 Parallel. Add the values for the modes wanted.

parameters.name: single-point override
parameters.description: Typing a three-letter code such as end, mid, cen or int at a point prompt overrides the running snaps for that one pick.

parameters.name: APParent intersection
parameters.description: Snaps where two objects would intersect if extended, or where they cross visually in the current view without touching in 3D.

parameters.name: EXTension / PARallel
parameters.description: Tracking snaps: hover over an endpoint to get a temporary extension line, or over a line to align parallel to it.

parameters.name: AUTOSNAP
parameters.description: Bitcode controlling the marker, magnet, tooltip and polar/object snap tracking aids.

parameters.name: APBOX / OSNAPZ
parameters.description: APBOX shows the aperture box around the crosshairs; OSNAPZ 1 forces snapped points onto the current elevation, ignoring the object's Z - essential when snapping 2D work over 3D geometry.

tools.example:
; Script-safe way to set running snaps
-OSNAP
END,MID,CEN,INT,PER

; Same set as a bitcode: 1+2+4+8+32+128 = 175
(setvar "OSMODE" 175)

; Polite LISP routine: save, change, restore
(setq old (getvar "OSMODE"))
(setvar "OSMODE" 0)
(command "_LINE" '(0 0) '(100 0) "")
(setvar "OSMODE" old)
tools.notes: Turning on every snap at once makes picking unpredictable; a set of Endpoint, Midpoint, Center, Intersection and Perpendicular covers most work, with the rest used as single-point overrides. 3DOSNAP holds the separate running snaps for 3D objects (vertex, midpoint on edge, face, knot, perpendicular, nearest to face).

tools.name: DSETTINGS
tools.description: Open the Drafting Settings dialog, the single place where snap and grid, polar tracking, object snaps, 3D object snaps, dynamic input, quick properties and selection cycling are configured. Every status-bar toggle at the bottom of the window has its settings here, and right-clicking a status-bar button jumps straight to the relevant tab.
tools.usage:
DSETTINGS  (aliases DS, SE; also right-click a status bar toggle and choose Settings)
(tabs) Snap and Grid | Polar Tracking | Object Snap | 3D Object Snap | Dynamic Input | Quick Properties | Selection Cycling

parameters.name: Snap and Grid
parameters.description: Snap spacing and type, grid spacing, major line frequency and the adaptive grid options - the same settings as SNAP and GRID.

parameters.name: Polar Tracking
parameters.description: Increment angle (POLARANG), additional angles, and whether tracking is measured absolutely or relative to the last segment.

parameters.name: Object Snap
parameters.description: Running object snaps (OSMODE) and object snap tracking - the same settings as OSNAP.

parameters.name: 3D Object Snap
parameters.description: Running snaps for solids, surfaces and meshes: vertex, midpoint on edge, centre of face, knot, perpendicular and nearest to face (3DOSMODE).

parameters.name: Dynamic Input
parameters.description: Pointer input, dimensional input and the dynamic prompts shown at the cursor; held in DYNMODE with DYNPICOORDS deciding whether typed coordinates are relative or absolute.

parameters.name: Quick Properties / Selection Cycling
parameters.description: Whether the Quick Properties panel appears on selection, and whether overlapping objects offer a cycling list when picked.

tools.example:
; Dialog route
DSETTINGS
(Polar Tracking tab: increment angle 15, additional angle 22.5)
(Object Snap tab: Endpoint, Midpoint, Center, Intersection)

; Script route - same result without a dialog
POLARANG
15
AUTOSNAP
55
-OSNAP
END,MID,CEN,INT
tools.notes: Scripts cannot drive the dialog, so set the underlying system variables (SNAPUNIT, GRIDUNIT, OSMODE, POLARANG, AUTOSNAP, DYNMODE) directly instead. These settings are stored partly in the drawing and partly in the user profile, so a template alone does not guarantee everyone has the same aids on.

tools.name: OPTIONS
tools.description: Open the Options dialog: the application-wide preferences covering support and template file paths, display and colours, open and save behaviour, plotting defaults, system and performance settings, user preferences, drafting aids, 3D modelling, selection and profiles. Most of the settings map to system variables, and the whole collection can be saved as a named profile and exported to an .arg file for deployment.
tools.usage:
OPTIONS  (alias OP; also right-click in the drawing area with nothing selected and choose Options)
(tabs) Files | Display | Open and Save | Plot and Publish | System | User Preferences | Drafting | 3D Modeling | Selection | Profiles

parameters.name: Files
parameters.description: Support file search path, working support file folder, template and plot style folders, and the location of the automatic save and drawing recovery files.

parameters.name: Open and Save
parameters.description: Default DWG save format, incremental save percentage, automatic save interval (SAVETIME), backup copies (ISAVEBAK) and xref demand loading.

parameters.name: Display
parameters.description: Colour scheme, crosshair size, layout elements, and the display resolution settings that include arc smoothness (VIEWRES) and rendered object smoothness (FACETRES).

parameters.name: Selection
parameters.description: Pickbox size (PICKBOX), grip size and colours, noun/verb selection (PICKFIRST), use Shift to add (PICKADD), window selection method and selection cycling.

parameters.name: Profiles
parameters.description: Named sets of all these options; export to an .arg file to roll a standard configuration out to a team, or run acad.exe with the /p switch to start in a given profile.

parameters.name: 3D Modeling
parameters.description: 3D crosshair display, dynamic UCS, default visual style and lighting for new 3D views, and the walk and fly settings.

tools.example:
; Most Options settings are also system variables that scripts can set
SAVETIME
10
PICKBOX
5
PICKADD
2
ISAVEBAK
0
FILEDIA
1

; Add a folder to the support path from AutoLISP
(setq p (vla-get-Files (vla-get-Preferences (vlax-get-acad-object))))
(vla-put-SupportPath p (strcat (vla-get-SupportPath p) ";C:\\standards\\lisp"))
tools.notes: Options are per-user and stored in the profile and the registry, not in the drawing, so they do not travel with a DWG. Settings that do belong to the drawing - units, limits, dimension and text styles - must be set in the template instead.

tools.name: CUI
tools.description: Open the Customize User Interface editor, where the ribbon tabs and panels, toolbars, pull-down menus, shortcut menus, keyboard shortcuts, double-click actions and workspaces are defined. Customisation lives in CUIx files: the main acad.cuix, optional partial files for an office standard, and an enterprise file that can be made read-only on a network share. Commands here are macros - strings such as ^C^C_LINE that AutoCAD types for you.
tools.usage:
CUI
(editor) Customizations In <file> tree | Command List | Properties and Macro panes

CUILOAD / CUIUNLOAD      ; load or unload a partial CUIx from the command line
CUIEXPORT / CUIIMPORT    ; move customisations between files
WORKSPACE                ; set or save the current workspace

parameters.name: Macro
parameters.description: The command string run by a button. ^C^C cancels twice first, an underscore prefix makes it language independent, and a backslash pauses for user input.

parameters.name: Partial CUIx
parameters.description: A separate customisation file loaded alongside the main one, so an office standard can be updated without touching acad.cuix.

parameters.name: Enterprise CUIx
parameters.description: A shared, normally read-only customisation file defined in OPTIONS; it loads before the main file.

parameters.name: Workspaces
parameters.description: Named arrangements of ribbon tabs, palettes and toolbars. WORKSPACE sets or saves one, WSCURRENT holds the current name, and WSSAVE saves the present arrangement.

parameters.name: Keyboard shortcuts
parameters.description: Accelerator keys and temporary override keys, edited in the same tree.

parameters.name: Command List
parameters.description: Every command known to the interface, where new commands are created and given a name, macro, tooltip and image before being dragged into a panel.

tools.example:
; Create a command in the CUI Command List with this macro:
;   ^C^C_-LAYER;_M;DIMENSIONS;_C;2;;;
; then drag it onto a ribbon panel.

; Load an office partial customisation file
CUILOAD
C:/standards/office.cuix

; Switch and save workspaces
WORKSPACE
S
DRAFTING_2D
(setvar "WSCURRENT" "Drafting & Annotation")
tools.notes: Command aliases are not edited here - they live in acad.pgp, which AutoCAD reloads with REINIT. Keep customisation in a partial or enterprise CUIx so that an AutoCAD upgrade, which replaces acad.cuix, does not wipe it out.

tools.name: ADCENTER
tools.description: Open DesignCenter: a browser that looks inside any drawing on disk and lets you drag its blocks, layers, linetypes, text styles, dimension styles, table styles, layouts and xrefs into the current drawing. It is the standard way to pull content out of an existing project file without opening it, and the Search tab finds a block by name across a whole folder tree.
tools.usage:
ADCENTER  (alias ADC; Ctrl+2; close with ADCCLOSE)
(palette tabs) Folders | Open Drawings | History
(tree) drawing > Blocks / Dimstyles / Layers / Layouts / Linetypes / Multileaderstyles / Tablestyles / Textstyles / Xrefs
(drag an item into the drawing, or right-click and choose Insert / Add)

parameters.name: Folders tab
parameters.description: Browse the file system and look inside any DWG, DWT or DXF without opening it.

parameters.name: Open Drawings tab
parameters.description: Copy content between the drawings already open in this session.

parameters.name: Search
parameters.description: Find blocks, layers, styles or drawings by name, date or description across a folder tree.

parameters.name: Drag versus double-click
parameters.description: Dragging a block inserts it at the drop point at scale 1; double-clicking opens the Insert dialog where scale and rotation can be set.

parameters.name: Add to Favorites
parameters.description: Puts a shortcut to a folder in the DesignCenter Favorites folder so a block library is one click away.

parameters.name: Create Tool Palette
parameters.description: Right-clicking a drawing or a Blocks node builds a tool palette containing all of its blocks in one step.

tools.example:
ADCENTER
; Folders tab > C:/standards/blocks/valves.dwg > Blocks
; drag VALVE_GATE into the drawing

; Import a whole layer standard from a template
; Folders tab > C:/standards/office.dwt > Layers
; select all, right-click, Add Layer(s)

; Command-line equivalent for one block
-INSERT
VALVE_GATE=C:/standards/blocks/valves.dwg
0,0
1
1
0
tools.notes: TOOLPALETTES (Ctrl+3) is the companion palette for content used every day, and palettes can be shared from a network folder set in OPTIONS. SHEETSET (Ctrl+4) manages the layouts of a whole project as a set with automatic sheet numbering and fields; both are usually populated from DesignCenter in the first place.

tools.name: SELECT
tools.description: Build a selection set without running any other command. The set is remembered and can be recalled at any later Select objects prompt with the Previous option, which is how a hard-to-make selection is reused across several editing commands. All of the standard selection options - Window, Crossing, Fence, WPolygon, CPolygon, ALL, Last, Add, Remove - are available here and at every other Select objects prompt.
tools.usage:
SELECT
Select objects: [Window/Last/Crossing/BOX/ALL/Fence/WPolygon/CPolygon/Group/Add/Remove/Multiple/Previous/Undo/AUto/SIngle/SUbobject/Object]
Select objects: Enter

; Reuse the set in the next command
ERASE
P

parameters.name: Window (W) / Crossing (C)
parameters.description: Window selects only objects wholly inside the box; Crossing also takes anything the box touches.

parameters.name: WPolygon (WP) / CPolygon (CP) / Fence (F)
parameters.description: Irregular selection: a closed polygon in window or crossing mode, or a fence line that selects everything it crosses.

parameters.name: ALL / Last (L) / Previous (P)
parameters.description: Everything in the drawing except on frozen or locked layers; the most recently created object; the previous selection set.

parameters.name: Add (A) / Remove (R)
parameters.description: Switch between adding to and removing from the set; Shift+pick does the same interactively.

parameters.name: SUbobject (SU) / Object (O)
parameters.description: Select faces, edges and vertices of 3D solids (also done by holding Ctrl while picking), then switch back to whole objects.

parameters.name: PICKFIRST / PICKADD
parameters.description: PICKFIRST allows selecting before typing a command; PICKADD controls whether each pick adds to the set or replaces it.

tools.example:
; Build a difficult selection once, then use it twice
SELECT
F
0,0
5000,3000

R
(pick the two objects to exclude)

CHPROP
P

LA
STRUCTURE

MOVE
P

0,0
0,0,500

; The AutoLISP equivalent builds the set directly
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((8 . "WALLS") (0 . "LINE"))))
tools.notes: Previous refers to the last selection set, not the last command, and it is cleared when you move between model space and paper space. In AutoLISP, (ssget) with filter lists is almost always better than driving SELECT, because it needs no user interaction and never depends on what is visible on screen.

tools.name: QSELECT
tools.description: Build a selection set from a property filter: choose an object type, a property of that type, an operator and a value, and every matching object is selected. It is the everyday tool for jobs such as 'select every circle with radius 4' or 'select all text on the OLD layer', and the result can replace or be appended to the current selection. Applying it to the current selection instead of the whole drawing lets filters be stacked.
tools.usage:
QSELECT  (also on the right-click menu and at the top of the Properties palette)
(dialog) Apply to: Entire drawing | Current selection
         Object type: Multiple | <a single type present in the drawing>
         Properties: <property list for that type>
         Operator: = | <> | > | < | Select All | *Wildcard Match
         Value: <value>
         How to apply: Include in new selection set | Exclude from new selection set
         [ ] Append to current selection set

parameters.name: Apply to
parameters.description: Entire drawing, or the current selection - the way to narrow a set down with a second filter.

parameters.name: Object type
parameters.description: Only the object types actually present are listed; Multiple searches across all types using the general properties.

parameters.name: Properties
parameters.description: Both general properties (layer, colour, linetype, lineweight) and type-specific ones (radius, area, text style, block name).

parameters.name: Operator
parameters.description: Equals, not equal to, greater than, less than, Select All, and *Wildcard Match for text values using * and ? patterns.

parameters.name: Exclude from new selection set
parameters.description: Inverts the filter, selecting everything that does not match - the fastest way to select all but one layer.

parameters.name: Append to current selection set
parameters.description: Adds the matches to what is already selected instead of replacing it.

tools.example:
; Select every circle of radius 4 on layer HOLES, then change them
QSELECT
; Apply to: Entire drawing
; Object type: Circle
; Properties: Radius   Operator: =   Value: 4
; Include in new selection set
CHPROP
P

LA
DRILL


; The scripted equivalent needs no dialog
(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "CIRCLE") (8 . "HOLES") (40 . 4.0))))
(command "_.CHPROP" ss "" "_LA" "DRILL" "")
tools.notes: QSELECT is a dialog and so cannot be driven from a script; use (ssget "_X" <filter list>) in AutoLISP for the same job unattended. For conditions that need AND, OR and NOT logic, or that must be saved and reused, use FILTER instead.

tools.name: FILTER
tools.description: Build a selection filter from a list of conditions combined with the logical grouping operators AND, OR, XOR and NOT, and save it under a name for reuse. It goes beyond QSELECT because conditions can be nested and because named filters persist between drawings in the filter.nfl file. Run it transparently at any Select objects prompt to filter the objects you then select.
tools.usage:
FILTER  (alias FI)
(dialog) Select Filter: <property> <operator> <value> -> Add to List
         Add Selected Object <  |  Substitute  |  Edit Item  |  Delete
         Named filters: Current / Save As / Delete Current Filter List
         Apply

; Transparent use inside a command
ERASE
'FILTER
(choose a named filter, Apply)
Select objects: ALL

parameters.name: Select Filter
parameters.description: Property to test: object type, layer, colour, linetype, block name, text value, thickness, elevation and many numeric properties.

parameters.name: operators
parameters.description: Numeric properties take = , != , < , <= , > and >= ; the value field accepts wildcards for names and strings.

parameters.name: Grouping operators
parameters.description: **Begin AND / **End AND and the OR, XOR and NOT equivalents, which nest to build compound conditions.

parameters.name: Add Selected Object
parameters.description: Picks an object in the drawing and loads all of its properties into the filter list as a starting point.

parameters.name: Save As / Named filters
parameters.description: Stores the list under a name in filter.nfl so it is available in every drawing on that machine.

parameters.name: Apply
parameters.description: Returns to the Select objects prompt; only objects you then select that pass the filter go into the set.

tools.example:
; Named filter: circles on HOLES, or any arc on the same layer
; **Begin OR
;   **Begin AND
;     Object = Circle
;     Layer  = HOLES
;   **End AND
;   **Begin AND
;     Object = Arc
;     Layer  = HOLES
;   **End AND
; **End OR
; Save As: HOLE_GEOMETRY

ERASE
'FILTER
(Current: HOLE_GEOMETRY, Apply)
ALL
tools.notes: A filter restricts what your subsequent selection can pick up - you still have to select, typically with ALL or a window. QSELECT is quicker for a single condition; FILTER earns its place when the condition is compound or is needed again tomorrow.

tools.name: SELECTSIMILAR
tools.description: Select every object in the drawing that is of the same type as, and matches the chosen properties of, the objects already picked. The Settings option decides which properties must match - layer is the usual one - so picking one dimension on a layer and running the command gathers all of them. It is the fastest informal selection tool in AutoCAD and needs no dialog or filter list.
tools.usage:
SELECTSIMILAR
Select objects or [SEttings]: <objects> | SE
Select objects: Enter
(SEttings dialog) match on: Color / Layer / Linetype / Linetype scale / Lineweight / Plot style / Object style / Name

parameters.name: SEttings (SE)
parameters.description: Choose which properties must match. With nothing ticked, every object of the same type is selected.

parameters.name: Layer
parameters.description: The most useful match property: selects all objects of that type on the same layer.

parameters.name: Object style
parameters.description: Matches the named style of styled objects - text style, dimension style, table style, multileader style.

parameters.name: Name
parameters.description: Matches the name of named references: block name, xref name, image name. This is how every insertion of one block is selected.

parameters.name: SELECTSIMILARMODE
parameters.description: System variable holding the same settings as a bitcode, so a script or LISP routine can set them.

tools.example:
; Select every insertion of one block and change its layer
SELECTSIMILAR
SE
(tick Layer and Name)

(pick one block reference)

CHPROP
P

LA
EQUIPMENT


; ADDSELECTED draws a new object matching the one picked
ADDSELECTED
(pick an existing dimension)
(place the new dimension - same style and layer)
tools.notes: The search covers the current space only, so objects in paper space are not gathered while you are in model space. Where the match needs to be on a value rather than a property - all circles below a radius, say - use QSELECT.

tools.name: ADDSELECTED
tools.description: Create a new object of the same type and with the same general properties as an object you pick. The new object inherits layer, colour, linetype, and for styled objects the style - text style and height, dimension style, hatch pattern and scale, block name - and then prompts normally for its geometry. It saves setting the current layer and style before drawing something that has to match existing work.
tools.usage:
ADDSELECTED  (also on the right-click menu: Add Selected)
Select object: <object to match>
(the matching creation command starts, already configured)
<normal prompts for the new object>

parameters.name: Select object
parameters.description: The template object. Its type decides which command runs - pick an MTEXT and MTEXT starts, pick a hatch and HATCH starts.

parameters.name: inherited properties
parameters.description: Layer, colour, linetype, lineweight and transparency of the picked object, regardless of the current settings.

parameters.name: inherited style
parameters.description: Text style and height, dimension style, multileader style, table style, or hatch pattern, scale and angle.

parameters.name: blocks
parameters.description: Picking a block reference starts INSERT with that block name, scale and rotation already set.

tools.example:
; Add another note that matches an existing one exactly
ADDSELECTED
(pick an existing note)
(the MTEXT command starts on the same layer, style and height)
120,80
200,60
SECOND NOTE TEXT

; Add another instance of a block already in the drawing
ADDSELECTED
(pick a block reference)
300,150
tools.notes: It is the creation counterpart of MATCHPROP, which pushes properties onto objects that already exist. Neither changes the current layer or style, so after the command the drawing settings are exactly as they were.

tools.name: ISOLATEOBJECTS / HIDEOBJECTS / UNISOLATEOBJECTS
tools.description: Temporarily hide everything except the selected objects, hide just the selected objects, or bring everything back. Unlike freezing layers this works on individual objects regardless of layer, so a single pipe run or one piece of a dense assembly can be worked on in isolation and restored in one click. The lightbulb icon on the status bar shows when anything is hidden.
tools.usage:
ISOLATEOBJECTS  (alias ISOLATE)
Select objects: <objects to keep visible>

HIDEOBJECTS
Select objects: <objects to hide>

UNISOLATEOBJECTS  (alias UNISOLATE)   ; redisplay everything hidden this way

; Status bar: the lightbulb icon at the bottom right offers the same three options

parameters.name: ISOLATEOBJECTS
parameters.description: Hides everything except the selection.

parameters.name: HIDEOBJECTS
parameters.description: Hides the selection and leaves everything else visible.

parameters.name: UNISOLATEOBJECTS
parameters.description: Ends isolation and redisplays every object hidden by these commands.

parameters.name: OBJECTISOLATIONMODE
parameters.description: 0 - isolation is lost when the drawing is saved and reopened; 1 - the hidden state is stored with the drawing and persists between sessions.

parameters.name: scope
parameters.description: Hidden objects are still in the drawing: they are not selected by ALL, are not plotted, and are not affected by editing commands while hidden.

tools.example:
; Work on one system in a congested drawing
ISOLATEOBJECTS
(select the pipe run)

; ... edit it ...

UNISOLATEOBJECTS

; Make isolation survive a save and reopen
OBJECTISOLATIONMODE
1
tools.notes: With OBJECTISOLATIONMODE set to 1, a drawing can be handed on with objects still hidden and the next person may not realise why geometry is missing - run UNISOLATEOBJECTS before issuing. LAYISO and LAYUNISO do the same job at layer level.

tools.name: BOX
tools.description: Create a rectangular 3D solid from two opposite corners of the base and a height, or from a centre point, or as a cube. The base is always drawn parallel to the XY plane of the current UCS, so the UCS - or a dynamic UCS picked off an existing face - determines its orientation. It is the starting primitive for most machined-part and building-mass models.
tools.usage:
BOX
Specify first corner or [Center]: <point> | C
Specify other corner or [Cube/Length]: <point> | C | L
Specify height or [2Point]: <height> | 2P

parameters.name: Center (C)
parameters.description: Define the box from the centre of its volume rather than a base corner.

parameters.name: Cube (C)
parameters.description: All three dimensions equal to the length given.

parameters.name: Length (L)
parameters.description: Type the length, width and height instead of picking; length follows the X axis of the current UCS unless a direction is picked.

parameters.name: 2Point (2P)
parameters.description: Define the height as the distance between two picked points, which is how a solid is made to match existing geometry.

parameters.name: negative height
parameters.description: A negative height builds the box downwards from the base plane.

parameters.name: ISOLINES / FACETRES / DISPSILH
parameters.description: Display controls for solids: ISOLINES is the number of contour lines drawn on curved faces in wireframe, FACETRES the smoothness of shaded and hidden-line output, and DISPSILH 1 shows silhouette edges and suppresses the isolines.

tools.example:
; 100 x 60 x 40 block at the origin
BOX
0,0,0
L
100
60
40

; A 25 cube centred on a point
BOX
C
200,100,0
C
25

; Make solids look smooth before rendering
ISOLINES
16
FACETRES
5
DISPSILH
1
REGEN
tools.notes: Primitives are only a starting point; real parts are built by adding and cutting with UNION, SUBTRACT and INTERSECT and refined with SOLIDEDIT, FILLETEDGE and CHAMFEREDGE. Set the visual style with VSCURRENT (Conceptual, Shaded with edges, Realistic) to see what you are building.

tools.name: CYLINDER / CONE
tools.description: Create a cylinder or a cone as a 3D solid from a circular or elliptical base and a height. Both accept the same base definitions as the CIRCLE command - centre and radius, 3P, 2P and tangent-tangent-radius - and both can be given an axis endpoint instead of a height so the axis points in any direction. CONE additionally takes a top radius, which turns it into a truncated cone, the standard shape for reducers, chamfered bosses and hoppers.
tools.usage:
CYLINDER  (alias CYL)
Specify center point of base or [3P/2P/Ttr/Elliptical]: <point> | 3P | 2P | T | E
Specify base radius or [Diameter]: <radius> | D
Specify height or [2Point/Axis endpoint]: <height> | 2P | A

CONE
Specify center point of base or [3P/2P/Ttr/Elliptical]: <point>
Specify base radius or [Diameter]: <radius>
Specify height or [2Point/Axis endpoint/Top radius]: <height> | 2P | A | T

parameters.name: Elliptical (E)
parameters.description: Build the solid on an elliptical base defined by its axis endpoints, giving an elliptical cylinder or cone.

parameters.name: Axis endpoint (A)
parameters.description: Point the axis at any 3D location, so the solid is created at an angle without changing the UCS.

parameters.name: Top radius (T)
parameters.description: CONE only: a non-zero top radius produces a truncated cone (a frustum) rather than a point.

parameters.name: 2Point (2P)
parameters.description: Take the height from the distance between two picked points.

parameters.name: Diameter (D)
parameters.description: Enter a diameter instead of a radius, which is how machined features are usually dimensioned.

parameters.name: 3P / 2P / Ttr
parameters.description: The same base-circle constructions as CIRCLE: three points, two diameter points, or tangent to two objects with a given radius.

tools.example:
; 20 mm diameter pin, 80 long
CYLINDER
0,0,0
D
20
80

; Drill a 10 mm hole through a block
BOX
0,0,0
L
100
60
40
CYLINDER
50,30,0
D
10
40
SUBTRACT
(select the box)

(select the cylinder)

; Reducer: 50 down to 30 over 40
CONE
200,0,0
25
T
15
40
tools.notes: A cylinder created with an Axis endpoint is the quickest way to model an inclined bolt or shaft without rotating the UCS. For a hole that must follow a curved path, sweep a circle along it with SWEEP and subtract the result.

tools.name: SPHERE / TORUS / WEDGE / PYRAMID
tools.description: The remaining 3D solid primitives. SPHERE takes a centre and a radius; TORUS takes a centre, the radius of the ring and the radius of the tube, so a tube radius larger than the ring radius produces a self-intersecting lemon shape. WEDGE takes exactly the same prompts as BOX and slopes along the X axis of the current UCS, and PYRAMID builds a 3 to 32 sided pyramid or, with a top radius, a truncated one.
tools.usage:
SPHERE
Specify center point or [3P/2P/Ttr]: <point>
Specify radius or [Diameter]: <radius> | D

TORUS  (alias TOR)
Specify center point or [3P/2P/Ttr]: <point>
Specify radius or [Diameter]: <ring radius>
Specify tube radius or [2Point/Diameter]: <tube radius>

WEDGE  (alias WE)
Specify first corner or [Center]: <point>
Specify other corner or [Cube/Length]: <point> | C | L
Specify height or [2Point]: <height>

PYRAMID  (alias PYR)
4 sides  Circumscribed
Specify center point of base or [Edge/Sides]: <point> | E | S
Specify base radius or [Inscribed]: <radius> | I
Specify height or [2Point/Axis endpoint/Top radius]: <height> | 2P | A | T

parameters.name: SPHERE radius / Diameter
parameters.description: Size of the sphere; 3P, 2P and Ttr define it from points or tangency exactly as for a circle.

parameters.name: TORUS radius and tube radius
parameters.description: Ring radius measured from the centre of the torus to the centre of the tube, then the radius of the tube itself. A negative ring radius with a larger tube radius gives a lemon-shaped solid.

parameters.name: WEDGE
parameters.description: Same prompts as BOX. The slope always falls along the positive X axis of the current UCS, so rotate the UCS or the finished solid to face it elsewhere.

parameters.name: PYRAMID Sides (S)
parameters.description: Number of base sides, 3 to 32.

parameters.name: PYRAMID Inscribed / Circumscribed
parameters.description: Whether the base radius is measured to the corners or to the middle of the flats - the same distinction as in POLYGON.

parameters.name: PYRAMID Top radius (T)
parameters.description: Non-zero top radius creates a truncated pyramid, used for hoppers, plinths and transitions.

tools.example:
; Ball end: 12 radius sphere on the end of a shaft
SPHERE
0,0,80
12

; O-ring: 50 mean diameter, 3 mm cord
TORUS
0,0,0
25
1.5

; Wedge 100 long, 50 wide, 30 high
WEDGE
0,0,0
L
100
50
30

; Truncated hexagonal hopper
PYRAMID
S
6

0,0,0

100
T
40
150
tools.notes: Solids created as primitives keep a history when SOLIDHIST is 1, so their original defining dimensions remain editable in the Properties palette; with SOLIDHIST 0 the result is a plain solid. MESHSMOOTH converts a solid or surface into a mesh object that can then be smoothed and creased for free-form shapes.

tools.name: POLYSOLID
tools.description: Draw a solid with a rectangular profile of a set height and width by picking points as if drawing a polyline, or convert an existing line, 2D polyline, arc or circle into one. It is the direct way to model walls, kerbs, upstands and ducts, because the path can include arcs and the justification decides which side of the picked line the thickness falls on.
tools.usage:
POLYSOLID  (alias PSOLID)
Height = 4.0000, Width = 0.2500, Justification = Center
Specify start point or [Object/Height/Width/Justify] <Object>: <point> | O | H | W | J
Specify next point or [Arc/Undo]: <point> | A | U
Specify next point or [Arc/Close/Undo]: C | U | Enter

parameters.name: Object (O)
parameters.description: Convert an existing line, 2D polyline, arc or circle into a polysolid, using the current height and width.

parameters.name: Height (H)
parameters.description: Height of the solid; stored in PSOLHEIGHT and remembered between commands.

parameters.name: Width (W)
parameters.description: Thickness of the profile; stored in PSOLWIDTH.

parameters.name: Justify (J)
parameters.description: Left, Center or Right - which side of the picked path the width is measured from, exactly like multiline justification.

parameters.name: Arc (A)
parameters.description: Switch to arc segments while drawing, with Close, Direction, Line, Second point and Undo options.

tools.example:
; 200 mm wall, 2700 high, centred on the picked line
POLYSOLID
H
2700
W
200
J
C
0,0
5000,0
5000,4000
0,4000
C

; Convert an existing plan polyline into walls
POLYSOLID
O
(select the polyline)
tools.notes: Because the result is an ordinary 3D solid, openings are cut by subtracting a box: draw the opening as a box and run SUBTRACT. Converting with the Object option deletes the source object when DELOBJ says so, so check that variable before converting a plan you still need.

tools.name: EXTRUDE
tools.description: Create a 3D solid or surface by extruding a profile through a height, along a direction, or along a path. Closed profiles - circles, closed polylines, regions - give solids; open profiles give surfaces, and the MOde option forces one or the other. The Taper angle option gives draft, which is how moulded and cast features are modelled, and a negative angle flares outwards.
tools.usage:
EXTRUDE  (alias EXT)
Current wire frame density: ISOLINES=4, Closed profiles creation mode = Solid
Select objects to extrude or [MOde]: <objects> | MO
Select objects to extrude: Enter
Specify height of extrusion or [Direction/Path/Taper angle/Expression]: <height> | D | P | T | E

parameters.name: MOde (MO)
parameters.description: SOlid or SUrface - what a closed profile produces. Open profiles always produce surfaces.

parameters.name: Path (P)
parameters.description: Extrude along a line, arc, polyline, spline, helix or the edge of a solid. The path should not lie in the plane of the profile.

parameters.name: Taper angle (T)
parameters.description: Draft angle; positive tapers inwards as it extrudes, negative flares outwards. Too large an angle for the height makes the profile close on itself and the command fails.

parameters.name: Direction (D)
parameters.description: Give the extrusion direction and length by two points, so the result leans without changing the UCS.

parameters.name: Expression (E)
parameters.description: Drive the height with a formula referencing constraint parameters, keeping the model parametric.

parameters.name: DELOBJ
parameters.description: Controls whether the profile and path are deleted when the solid is created: 0 keeps everything, 1 deletes the profile, 2 deletes profile and path, 3 prompts. Set it to 0 while developing a model so the profiles can be reused.

tools.example:

tools.name: REVOLVE
tools.description: Create a solid or surface by revolving a profile about an axis. The axis can be two picked points, an existing object, or the X, Y or Z axis of the current UCS, and the angle can be anything up to a full 360 degrees with an optional start angle. It is the natural command for shafts, bottles, flanges, pulleys and any turned part, because the profile is just the half-section of the finished item.

parameters.name: X / Y / Z

parameters.name: STart angle (ST)
parameters.description: Offset the start of the revolution from the plane of the profile, which is how a partial revolve is positioned.

parameters.name: Reverse (R)
parameters.description: Revolve in the opposite direction.

parameters.name: DELOBJ

tools.name: SWEEP

Unlike EXTRUDE Path, the profile does not have to sit on the path: by default it is moved to the start of the path and set perpendicular to it. The Twist and Scale options make it the command for springs, handrails, tapered ducts and threads, and the path may be a 3D polyline, spline or helix.

tools.name: LOFT
tools.description: Create a solid or surface through a series of cross sections, optionally controlled by guide curves or a single path. The sections are used in the order you select them, which is the most common source of twisted results. It is the command for transitions, boat hulls, ducts that change shape and any form that is defined by a set of stations rather than one profile.

parameters.name: Path (P)

parameters.name: Settings (S)

parameters.name: DELOBJ

tools.name: PRESSPULL
tools.description: Push or pull a bounded area, a closed object, or the face of an existing solid to create or modify a 3D solid. It detects a closed area from the surrounding geometry the way HATCH does, so a shape drawn with overlapping lines can be turned into a solid without first making a region. Pulling outwards adds material and pushing inwards removes it, which makes it the fastest way to cut a pocket or a hole into an existing solid.

parameters.description: A closed region detected from surrounding geometry, exactly as HATCH would find it - the boundary need not be a single object.

parameters.name: closed object
parameters.description: A circle, closed polyline, region or 2D solid picked directly.

parameters.name: face of a solid
parameters.description: Picking a planar face extends or shortens the solid there; picking a face inside a pocket deepens it.

parameters.name: Multiple (M)
parameters.description: Keep picking areas and press or pull each one without restarting the command.

parameters.name: negative distance
parameters.description: Pushing into a solid subtracts material, so a circle drawn on a face becomes a hole in one operation.

parameters.name: Ctrl while dragging
parameters.description: Holding Ctrl during a face drag offsets the adjacent faces with it instead of only the face picked.

tools.name: UNION / SUBTRACT / INTERSECT
tools.description: The Boolean operations that combine 3D solids, surfaces and 2D regions. UNION merges the selected objects into one, SUBTRACT removes the second set from the first, and INTERSECT keeps only the volume the objects have in common. Together with the primitives and EXTRUDE they account for most solid modelling in AutoCAD, and they work equally on regions for 2D section properties.

parameters.name: INTERSECT
parameters.description: Keeps only the common volume and deletes the originals; with regions it gives the overlapping area.

parameters.name: mixing types
parameters.description: Solids combine with solids and regions with regions; surfaces use SURFTRIM and the surface editing commands instead.

parameters.name: SOLIDHIST / SHOWHIST
parameters.description: SOLIDHIST 1 keeps a history of the original components inside a composite solid so they can still be selected and edited; SHOWHIST displays them.

parameters.name: INTERFERE

tools.description: Cut 3D solids and surfaces. SLICE permanently divides a solid with a plane, keeping one side or both as separate objects, and is the usual way to make a cutaway or to split a part for manufacture. SECTIONPLANE instead creates a section object that can be moved through the model as a live section, and which generates 2D or 3D section blocks on demand without destroying anything.

parameters.name: planar Object / Surface / Zaxis / View

parameters.description: Place the section plane aligned with Front, Back, Top, Bottom, Left or Right through the extents of the model in one step.

tools.description: Edit the faces, edges and body of an existing 3D solid: extrude, move, rotate, offset, taper, delete, copy or colour a face; copy or colour an edge; and imprint, separate, shell, clean or check the body. tools.description: Move, rotate and align objects in three dimensions. 3DMOVE and 3DROTATE display a gizmo that constrains the operation to one axis or one plane, which removes the guesswork of picking 3D points on screen. 3DALIGN takes up to three source points and their three destination points, so one object can be seated onto another's face in a single operation without setting a UCS.

tools.name: RENDER / MATBROWSER / LIGHT
tools.description: Produce a photorealistic image of a 3D model. MATBROWSER opens the Materials Browser where materials from the Autodesk library are dragged onto objects or layers, LIGHT creates point, spot, distant and web lights to replace the default lighting, and RENDER produces the image at a chosen quality and size in the render window. The sun and sky, driven by a geographic location and a date and time, give accurate shadows for architectural studies.
tools.usage:
MATBROWSER  (MATERIALS opens the same browser; MATEDITOR edits one material)
(drag a material onto an object, or use MATERIALATTACH to assign by layer)

LIGHT
Enter light type [Point/Spot/Web/Targetpoint/Freespot/freeweB/Distant] <Point>:
Specify source location <0,0,0>:
Enter an option to change [Name/Intensity factor/Status/Photometry/shadoW/Attenuation/filterColor/eXit] <eXit>:

RENDER  (alias RR)
; RENDERCROP renders a picked region; RENDERPRESETS sets the quality preset
; RENDERWINDOW reopens the image window

parameters.name: Materials Browser
parameters.description: The Autodesk material library plus the materials in this drawing; dragging one onto an object or a layer assigns it. MATERIALMAP adjusts how the texture is projected.

parameters.name: light types
parameters.description: Point lights radiate in all directions, spot lights have a hotspot and falloff cone, distant lights are parallel like the sun, and web lights use a photometric .ies distribution from a manufacturer.

parameters.name: DEFAULTLIGHTING
parameters.description: When 1, the default two-light rig is used and user lights are ignored; it must be set to 0 before created lights have any effect.

parameters.name: SUNPROPERTIES / GEOGRAPHICLOCATION
parameters.description: Sun status, date, time, intensity and sky illumination, and the latitude, longitude and north direction they are computed from - the basis of a shadow study.

parameters.name: RENDERPRESETS / render size
parameters.description: Quality presets from draft to high, the render duration or level, and the output resolution chosen in the render window.

parameters.name: VSCURRENT
parameters.description: Sets the viewport visual style - 2D Wireframe, Conceptual, Hidden, Shaded, Shaded with edges, Realistic - which is enough for most checking without a full render.

tools.example:
; Minimum viable render setup
VSCURRENT
R
DEFAULTLIGHTING
0
LIGHT
P
2000,-1500,3000

MATBROWSER
(drag a material onto the solid)
RENDER

; Shadow study for a given place and time
GEOGRAPHICLOCATION
(set latitude, longitude and north direction)
SUNPROPERTIES
(status on, date 21 June, time 15:00)
RENDER
tools.notes: Created lights do nothing while DEFAULTLIGHTING is 1 - the render simply looks flat and evenly lit, which is the usual reason a first render disappoints. LIGHTINGUNITS decides whether lights are generic or photometric (lumens and candelas); photometric units are required for meaningful daylight and luminaire results.
